items.title: US military weighs use of ‘mother of all bombs’ in potential future strikes on Iran, CNN says
items.content_html:
Oct 15 (Reuters) - The US military has developed strike plans ​that could include using ‌the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known ​as the "mother of ​all bombs", against Iranian energy ⁠infrastructure and nuclear sites ​if President Donald Trump ​orders renewed combat operations, CNN reported on Thursday citing US ​officials familiar with the ​matter.

The potential deployment of the largest ‌non-nuclear ⁠bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant escalation in the ​conflict, ​although ⁠officials familiar with military planning discussions ​told CNN questions remain ​over ⁠its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.

Reuters could ⁠not ​immediately verify the ​report.

items.title: US rejects recommendation for ICE body cams to be automatically activated
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The Trump administration ​has rejected a government watchdog's recommendation, opens new tab that US immigration officials should use technology that would ‌automatically activate body-worn cameras when an officer pulls their weapon or sets off a car siren.

Automatic activation of body-worn cameras was one of a number of recommendations outlined in a report released on Wednesday by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), an ​independent nonpartisan watchdog agency for Congress.

The recommendation comes as US agencies face mounting scrutiny over ​enforcement tactics used in an immigration crackdown that has included fatal shootings of two US ⁠citizens in Minneapolis, raising questions about officers' accountability.

The GAO report said US Immigration and Customs Enforcement ​and US Customs and Border Protection "should improve body-worn camera program management," adding that CBP and ICE have not ​updated their program plans since 2022 and 2024, respectively.

Covering the period from February 2025 until September this year, the report recommended that ICE implement additional controls to make sure that cameras are activated.

"We maintain that additional controls, such as ​automated camera activation, would provide greater assurance that body-worn cameras meet ICE's desired results for transparency, accountability, ​and public trust," the GAO said in the report.

The Department of Homeland Security, of which ICE is a part, said ‌in ⁠comments cited in the report that it did not agree with the recommendation, citing what it said were privacy and operational risks.

For ICE, automatic activation risked the possibility of inadvertent or false activations during routine movement, the DHS said in the report.

DHS also said in the report that inadvertent or false activations ​could result in the unauthorized ​recording of sensitive interactions ⁠with informants or victims, or the recording of bystanders engaged in free speech activities in areas where camera use is restricted.

ICE has been the face of ​President Donald Trump's deportation drive, which he says aims to improve domestic security. ​Rights advocates say ⁠the crackdown has violated due process and free speech rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

Responding to the GAO report's publication, a DHS spokesperson said on Wednesday ⁠ICE ​had acquired devices to equip all officers and agents with body ​cameras.

"Training required to equip individual officers remains ongoing and we expect to complete this training soon," the spokesperson said.

items.title: Anthropic to add US voting information to Claude before midterms
items.content_html:
Oct 14 (Reuters) - Anthropic said on Wednesday it would add official ​US voting information from nonprofit Democracy Works ‌and election results to its Claude AI chatbot later this month, ahead of the November midterms.

The AI company ​said its goal was to position Claude ​as a useful tool for political conversations, ⁠while preventing election-related abuse.

"Today, conversations that touch broadly ​on politics, public policy or social issues account ​for about 5.75% of all conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our consumer app," the company said ​in a statement, citing analysis of 250,000 US conversations.

The ​move comes as AI companies increasingly position chatbots as sources ‌of ⁠news and information, potentially helping Anthropic draw more users during the election cycle.

About 0.51% of Claude conversations are specifically about elections or voting, ​Anthropic said, adding ​that it ⁠expects political and election-related queries to rise as election day approaches.

Later ​this month, US users seeking voting logistics ​will ⁠receive answers drawn directly from Democracy Works’ database of state and local election sources.

Anthropic said requests ⁠for ​recommendations on how to vote ​were extremely rare, accounting for just 0.01% of U.S. conversations.

items.title: US Supreme Court again backs Republicans in clash over political ad rates
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court again sided with Republicans on Wednesday in the latest clash over a new Federal Communications Commission policy that gives party committees access ​to discounted TV and radio advertising rates long available to political candidates.

The court agreed to let the FCC, which is chaired by Trump ‌ally Brendan Carr, avoid a judicially imposed deadline that would have forced the agency to rule on a Democratic challenge to the policy before the November 3 midterm elections. The FCC joined two Republican committees in filing a request to the Supreme Court to lift the lower court's deadline.

The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. Liberal Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated ​they would have denied the request.

The FCC, which currently has a 2-1 Republican majority, modified its so-called "lowest unit charge" rule in March in a move ​seen as a boost to President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans. The president's party is seeking to retain control of Congress in the ⁠November 3 midterms.

"We are pleased the Supreme Court has granted the FCC's stay request. The court's decision is right on the law and avoids the specter of upending ​the rules for political ads right in the middle of an ongoing election," an FCC spokesperson said.

Chief Justice John Roberts had previously lifted the October 9 deadline that ​was given to the FCC by the Richmond-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals. The 4th Circuit has accused the FCC of repeated "delay tactics" in the case, and emphasized the need for an urgent ruling in the Democratic challenge given the looming election.

The Supreme Court's latest action marks the second time in recent weeks that it has addressed the FCC's policy, as major Republican ​committees head toward the midterms with a cash advantage over their Democratic counterparts.

In September, the court granted a request by the national Republican committees that support the party's candidates ​in Senate and House of Representatives races to revive the policy after the 4th Circuit blocked it. The justices in an 8-1 ruling said that the Democratic candidates must wait for ‌the FCC ⁠to rule before filing a challenge in court.

The FCC policy at issue requires broadcasters to charge discounted rates for airing certain political advertisements within 60 days of a general election, a window that opened this year on September 4.

A group of Democratic candidates including Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia in April challenged the policy through in-house proceedings at the FCC. When the agency took no action, the Democrats successfully challenged the policy in the 4th Circuit, a ruling that was later halted by the Supreme ​Court.

The 4th Circuit on October 7 ordered ​the FCC to issue a prompt ⁠ruling on the Democratic in-house challenge, more than five months after it was filed. In its 2-1 ruling, the 4th Circuit said its "willingness to tolerate the FCC's delay tactics is at an end."

The Republican committees in their Supreme Court filing accused ​the 4th Circuit of having "short-circuited" the FCC's review process.

The Democratic candidates, for their part, accused the FCC in court papers ​of engaging in "blatant procedural ⁠trench warfare to stave off judicial review of an unlawful agency directive until it is too late to matter."

The FCC policy gained greater significance after the Supreme Court in June struck down federal restrictions on spending coordinated between parties and their candidates, siding with Republican challengers including Vice President JD Vance. Since the June ruling, Republican committees have blown past the ⁠former limits ​ahead of the midterms.

The two Republican committees have exceeded the former national caps by more than $48 million, according ​to Federal Election Commission spending disclosures for July and August. Their Democratic counterparts also eclipsed the former limits, but by much less — just under $4 million.

The three main national Republican committees ended August with about $233 ​million in cash. Their Democratic counterparts held roughly $130 million but also carried nearly $18 million in debt, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

items.title: Ukraine's Zelenskiy says it is 'painful' when Trump chooses a different side
items.content_html:
LONDON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said in an interview on Wednesday ​that it was "painful" when Donald ‌Trump took another side in Ukraine's ongoing war with Russia, after the US President said ​Zelenskiy should be replaced.

Zelenskiy told ​Piers Morgan Uncensored: "It's painful when President Trump ⁠chooses one side, not our side."

He ​also said that he was OK ​with Trump being in the middle of Ukraine and Russia, but added: "If you are in the ​middle, you have to stay in ​the middle."

Asked if he felt betrayed by Trump, ‌who ⁠at the weekend called for Ukraine to get a new president having agreed to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, Zelenskiy ​replied: "Really, yes ... ​but it's ⁠a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or ​my feelings."

"It's a pity we ​are ⁠losing (a) strong partner," he added.

Zelenskiy also said: "We are not selling our country ... it's ⁠not ​about business for us, ​it's just our life and this is our country."

items.title: US inflation heats up in September; Fed rate hike this month back on table
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - US consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged, dealing another blow to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November 3 midterm elections and putting an interest rate increase later this month back on the radar.

The Consumer ​Price Index report from the Labor Department on Wednesday showed a broadening of price pressures beyond energy, raising concerns among economists that underlying inflation could be getting sticky. There was also an AI-related boost to inflation ‌last month. Financial markets now see the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision at its October 27-28 meeting as a closer call than before the data was released.

The report added to surveys this month that showed a further deterioration in consumer sentiment and a plunge in Trump's approval rating, driven by angst over the rising cost of living. A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed about 78% of Americans blamed Trump's policies, including tariffs and the Middle East conflict, for rising prices, which are outpacing wages.

"The inflation we're experiencing right now is largely the result of erratic policy from the executive branch," said Kyle Moore, chief economist at the ​Century Foundation, a progressive think tank. "Worse still, the directionless war in Iran continues to disrupt global supply chains. This administration has also been wholly unwilling to moderate the pace of the AI and data-center buildout."

The CPI rose 0.6% last ​month after climbing 0.4% in August, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said, in line with economists' expectations. In the 12 months through September, the CPI advanced 3.7% after rising 3.4% ⁠in August.

A 9.1% surge in gasoline prices accounted for more than half of the increase in the CPI over the month. The US-Israeli war with Iran is driving up energy prices. Other motor fuels, which include diesel, soared 11.9% last month and were up ​60.9% on a year-over-year basis. Diesel prices at the pump are at record highs, and there are fears that those costs will soon feed through to higher prices at the supermarket.

Food prices were unchanged after gaining 0.1% in both July and August. Grocery store prices ​dipped 0.1% over the month as beef prices dropped 1.0% and the cost of dairy and related products eased 0.9%. Egg prices declined 1.3%.

But prices for nonalcoholic beverages surged 0.9%, while fruits and vegetables cost 0.5% more, with banana prices shooting up 1.0%, in what could be early signs of rising trucking costs being passed on to consumers. Lettuce prices rebounded 3.9% as a cyclospora outbreak faded.

Grocery prices rose 1.8% on a year-over-year basis.

Average hourly earnings for all employees declined 0.7% in September from a year ago, after falling 0.3% in August, underscoring the squeeze on consumers in what economists call the ​bottom of a K-shaped economy.

Economists said this data raised doubts about whether consumers could maintain their robust pace of spending.

"While much of the lost purchasing power is due to rising energy costs, there is no reason to expect that to fade in ​the near term," said Eric Winograd, chief US economist at AllianceBernstein. "The bottom part of the K-shaped economy is losing ground, as anybody who has seen campaign ads on TV the last few weeks has heard."

With the cost of living rising, the Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living ‌adjustment for Social ⁠Security and Supplemental Security Income benefits for 2027. The programs benefit nearly 72 million Americans, including retirees, the disabled and certain widows, widowers and children. Social Security retirement benefits will, on average, increase by $75 per month.

Stocks on Wall Street fell. The dollar advanced versus a basket of currencies. Yields on US Treasury notes and bonds rose.

Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI rose 0.3% in September, matching the gain in August. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the so-called core CPI would increase 0.2%. The core CPI was lifted by a 0.4% advance in the cost of shelter, including hotel and motel rooms. Owners' equivalent rent, a measure of the amount homeowners would pay to rent or would earn from renting their property, rose 0.3%.

Airline fares rose 1.2% amid higher jet fuel prices. Consumers paid more for gardening ​and lawn care services, likely reflecting worker shortages amid a crackdown ​on undocumented immigrants. The costs of recreation and education also ⁠rose, as did those of hospital and dental services. Overall services prices increased 0.4%. They were also up 0.4% excluding energy.

Core goods prices rose 0.3%, pushed up by a 0.7% increase in the cost of used cars and trucks. Apparel prices climbed 0.3% and the cost of toys rebounded 4.2%, suggesting some lingering pass-through from tariffs. But prescription medication was cheaper.

Prices for computers and peripherals jumped ​1.3%, reflecting AI-related investment, while the cost of computer software and accessories rebounded 0.4%.

In the 12 months through September, core CPI inflation was 2.6%, compared with 2.4% in August.

The US central ​bank tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures ⁠Price Index for its 2% inflation target. Financial markets raised the chances of a rate hike at the Fed's meeting this month to roughly 37% from about 22% prior to the release of the CPI report, CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed.

The odds of a rate increase this month had diminished following underwhelming payroll gains in September as well as cooler-than-expected PCE inflation readings for July and August.

The Fed in September raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range, its first hike in three years, and flagged further increases in borrowing ⁠costs in the ​months ahead.

Most economists continue to expect the Fed will hold rates steady this month and raise them in December.

Based on the CPI data, economists' ​estimates for core PCE inflation ranged from 0.3% to 0.4%, which would mean a year-over-year reading of 3.1%. Producer price data being released on Thursday could impact those estimates. Core PCE inflation was 0.2% in August and 3.0% on a year-over-year basis.

"What is interesting is that the primary drivers of inflation are supply-side policies ​that are better addressed by the fiscal authority," said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. "However, that is not going to happen anytime soon, which leaves the Fed to address a re-establishment of price stability."

items.title: Ohio's working-class voters rethink support for Trump and the Republican Party
items.content_html:
WARREN, Ohio, Oct 14 (Reuters) - A decade after Republican Donald Trump peeled away working-class and union voters who had long been a cornerstone of Democratic support in Ohio, Democrats and labor leaders see an opening to win back some of them in the November 3 US elections.

Now midway through his second term, the president's magic appears to be losing at least ​some of its luster with blue-collar men and women as rising prices, the Iran war and concerns about his rhetoric prompt some voters to reconsider their support.

The state's reputation as a leading swing state began to fade in ‌2016 when Trump won strong support from working-class voters who felt their economic concerns were being heard, helping turn Ohio into a reliably Republican state.

Almost overnight, Ohio became rock-solid Republican. Ohio voted for the eventual winner in 14 straight presidential elections from 1964 until 2020 when Democrat Joe Biden won nationally but Ohio backed Trump.

A shift in Ohio toward Democrats could matter in elections that will help determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress during Trump's final two years in office or hand new leverage to Democrats over his agenda.

The stakes are high in Ohio, where Republicans are defending a US Senate seat and the governor's office. Two House ​races are rated "toss-ups." One, in northwestern Ohio, has long been held by a Democrat and the other, in northeastern Ohio, is Republican-held.

Trump is not on the ballot this time but has told supporters to act as if he is. It remains to ​be seen whether that could end up helping or hindering Republicans running in tough races.

Republican Senator Jon Husted is in a tight competition with Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown, while Democrat Amy Acton ⁠is challenging Republican Vivek Ramaswamy for an open governor's seat.

Trump campaigned with Husted and Ramaswamy in Youngstown on Monday to try to energize the Republican base.

Paul Ringold, a 48-year-old steel hauler and pastor of the mostly Black congregation at the ​Shalom Church of God and Christ in the city of Warren, embodies the uncertainty that Democrats hope could help them make inroads with working-class voters.

Ringold voted for Trump for president in 2016, Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump again in 2024, but said he remains undecided ​about whom to support for the US Senate, governor and other offices this year.

"I'm in the wilderness trying to find a place," he said.

Ringold said rising fuel and food prices and Trump's combative style have left him questioning some of the choices made by a president he once strongly supported.

"God knows we didn't vote for this," he said of inflation.

Like several voters interviewed by Reuters, Ringold also cited Trump's rhetoric. "I wish he would just tone down that rhetoric ... that old New York in-your-face 'I got you sucker'" persona, he said.

In early voting that began in Ohio last week, Democrats appeared to be more motivated than Republicans.

In Trumbull ​County, home to the city of Warren and many blue-collar jobs, a strong turnout during the first three days brought 1,224 Democrats to the polls, 559 Republicans and 453 with no known political affiliation, according to county data.

Paul Sracic, an Ohio-based senior fellow with the right-of-center ​Hudson Institute, said "working-class voters, if they are moving at all away from Trump, Brown is a safe landing spot for them" because of the former senator's populist record.

"Trump has done a good job of basically focusing on social issues with our guys," said Jose Arroyo, a United Steelworkers official who ‌engages in contract ⁠negotiations and labor relations for the sprawling labor union.

Trump "seemed to latch on sort of to the dissatisfaction of where the working man has gone. Pensions go away. Plants close. Livelihoods they've always known disappear."

The problem, he said, is that focusing primarily on hot-button social issues ignores advancing policies that would "improve the lives of working people" and actually turn them into law.

The 50,000 manufacturing jobs in 1990 in the Youngstown-Warren area fell to about 20,000 in 2026, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.

In recent years, the Mahoning Valley, long a powerhouse of the steel and automotive industries, has attracted a few new manufacturing plants. Arroyo said the Iran war has boosted domestic oil industry exploration, creating more demand for equipment made of steel. But he acknowledged that the war had also brought higher consumer prices.

When Trump began his second term in ​January 2025, he promptly fired two Democratic officials at the National Labor ​Relations Board and left the agency without the quorum required to ⁠take actions. That paralysis lasted for nearly a year.

Ohio AFL-CIO President Tim Burga cited what he called Trump's "dismantling" of the NLRB as having hindered union organizing efforts and made it harder to contest unfair labor practices and secure work contracts with companies.

"We were on a path for the first time in my lifetime, under the Biden administration, for having a national industrial policy," Burga said, but the Trump administration rolled ​much of it back. Biden and Congress enacted programs to spur investment in such industries as clean energy and semiconductors.

Trump's trade battles with Canada also were unhelpful to labor, he said.

Bill ​Callahan, 75, a self-described Democrat from Cortland, ⁠said some relatives who once backed Trump "are traveling back" toward Democrats because "they don't like (politicians) taking money out of their pockets."

A part-time warehouse worker from Cortland after a career at General Electric, he said he considered voting for Trump in 2016 but was put off by ethical concerns.

Others interviewed by Reuters said higher prices were not enough to change their vote.

Joe Scarabino, who co-owns a bait-and-tackle business with his wife Kathryn near Cortland, said the couple responded to higher fuel costs by raising delivery charges rather than product prices, thus having an impact on fewer customers and small business owners.

"We ⁠believe our Christian ​values are more than gas prices," he said. The couple declined to say who they support.

Retired coal-fired power plant worker Chuck Burns, 67, of Wellsville, credited Trump with ​reducing illegal immigration and boosting the value of his retirement investments. "He's done a good job ... he's got balls," Burns said.

Burns praised Trump's immigration restrictions at the southern border and said his retirement savings have increased in value since Biden left office.

Asked what issues worry him in this election season, Burns said, "It's just that Democrats – it's unbelievable some ​of the stuff that they want to do."

Asked to explain, Burns raised transgender issues. "Those poor people, they feel that way, that's fine, that's their business," he said. "They (Democrats) don't need to incorporate our young kids into that stuff."

items.title: US retirees to receive 3.6% Social Security increase in 2027
items.content_html:
Oct 14 (Reuters) - Some 76 million Americans receiving Social Security and Supplemental Security Income benefits will see their monthly ​payments rise 3.6% in 2027, accelerating from the prior ‌year's increase for a second straight year.

The Social Security Administration announced the annual cost-of-living adjustment to benefits on Wednesday ​after the Bureau of Labor Statistics published the Consumer ​Price Index for September.

The agency bases the annual ⁠increase, closely watched by retirees and others receiving ​benefits, on the average of the annual increase ​in the CPI for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, also known as the CPI-W index. That index rose 3.9% in September and ​averaged about 3.6% for the three months of ​July, August and September.

The increase takes effect in January for 72 million ‌Social ⁠Security recipients and on December 31, 2026, for nearly 7.3 million SSI beneficiaries. Some recipients receive both Social Security and SSI benefits.

For 2026, the increase was 2.8%.

Inflation accelerated ​again this year ​after the ⁠US and Israel attacked Iran, causing global energy market disruptions that have sent ​crude oil prices above $100 a barrel. More ​recently, refined ⁠petroleum products like diesel fuel have climbed to record highs and have contributed to a widening of ⁠inflationary ​pressures.

The more widely watched main CPI ​index rose 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August, BLS said.

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: US Justice Department threatens California over alleged noncitizen voters, letters show
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department on Tuesday gave California officials 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face ‌legal action, according to two letters reviewed by Reuters, part of an unprecedented effort to find evidence of voter fraud ahead of next month's elections.

The letters, written by acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter and addressed to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan, say the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people ​the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" and were sent mail-in ballots from California.

The letters demand that the state and county segregate returned mail-in ballots from voters ​on the Justice Department's list and not tabulate their votes "until citizenship has been determined." In cases where ballots have not been sent out ⁠yet, it orders California officials to withhold them from those on the list until their citizenship is confirmed.

The federal government "will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," according ​to the letters, if state and county officials do not follow its instructions.

"Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes," McCotter wrote.

The letters mark an escalation of the Trump administration's attempts to ​pressure states over alleged voting by non-US citizens and signal the Justice Department may be prepared to challenge ballots in the weeks leading up to the November 3 election, when Republicans will be defending their narrow majorities in Congress.

Justice Department spokeswoman Kiersten Pels confirmed the existence of the letters in a statement to Reuters, adding: "The department will take all necessary legal action to protect election integrity and ensure ​compliance with federal law.”

Representatives from the White House and the California secretary of state's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Logan also did not immediately respond.

The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that voting by non-US citizens is widespread, despite multiple studies showing it is rare.

Though states may have added more than 30,000 noncitizens to their voter ‌rolls since ⁠2000 due to software glitches and clerical errors, Reuters found in September, it was unclear how many had cast a ballot. Experts said the numbers were too small relative to the country’s 170 million registered voters to affect elections.

In July, the Justice Department sent letters to chief election officials in all 50 states warning they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls or cast ballots.

The department's Civil Rights Division has demanded nonpublic voter data, including voters' Social Security numbers or dates of birth, ​from nearly all states as part of its ​hunt for noncitizens on state rolls. ⁠It has sued 30 Democratic- and Republican-led states that refused to hand over their rolls, but has lost 26 of those cases without winning one.

Reuters reported last month that the Department of Homeland Security was using a commercial data broker to find sensitive voter information not included in ​publicly available rolls, which officials and experts warned could lead to citizens being falsely flagged as illegal voters and potentially detained.

Federal ​prosecutors have also ramped up ⁠prosecutions of noncitizens for allegedly voting in past elections or submitting fraudulent registrations, touting 16 new criminal cases on Monday.

Officials in Democratic-led California have tussled for months with the Trump administration over its attempts to intervene in election procedures over allegations of voter fraud.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin informed California officials on July 16 that the federal government believed the state had noncitizens ⁠on its voting ​rolls, according to the letter.

California could prove pivotal in deciding control of the US House of Representatives, ​especially after the state's voters approved a new congressional map that heavily favors Democrats as part of a nationwide redistricting sprint that began in Republican-led states.

Voters in Los Angeles will also weigh in on a ballot measure ​that would allow certain noncitizen legal residents to cast ballots in municipal elections.

items.title: FBI arrests Saudi OpenAI engineer over covert recording device, DOJ says
items.content_html:
Oct 13 (Reuters) - US federal agents arrested a Saudi national who was an OpenAI engineer and charged him with installing a hidden audio recording ‌device in an executive conference room at the AI company, the Justice Department said on Tuesday.

The case highlights growing security concerns around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete fiercely for the talent and technology that could confer economic and strategic advantages.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, had worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, the Justice ​Department said in a statement. An email sent to an address associated with that name did not elicit a response, and it ​was not immediately clear who his lawyer was.

OpenAI discovered the recording device plugged into a USB port on the ⁠back of a television in an executive conference room at one of its San Francisco buildings on September 30, according to the department.

The thumb-sized ​device, which had a microphone and could connect to a camera, was concealed in toilet paper, according to an FBI complaint. It was installed on or about ​September 28, while its stored data was encrypted and inaccessible. Investigators later found a similar customized device in Alfozan's personal bag.

OpenAI said in a post, opens new tab on X that it used its internal AI models to identify the person responsible for planting the device and trace its origins.

The company said it had evidence that the employee intended to place additional recording ​devices in sensitive areas of its offices to secretly record meetings.

"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating ​model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated," the company said.

OpenAI referred the matter to the FBI, which is continuing to investigate. The Saudi ‌embassy in ⁠the United States did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

"Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.

Alfozan also used an AI productivity agent to seek information about meeting-room calendars and capabilities for about a month through September 16, according to the FBI complaint. He has been a legal permanent ​resident of the US since September ​2020.

If convicted, Alfozan faces up to ⁠five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and three years of supervised release.

A LinkedIn profile showed that Alfozan studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the University of California, Berkeley. He previously worked at Meta and Microsoft, ​it said.

Reuters could not independently verify the details mentioned in his LinkedIn profile.

Separately, the Information reported, opens new tab that OpenAI was ​in early talks ⁠to acquire Trail of Bits, a startup that identifies and fixes vulnerabilities in open-source software. The talks were ongoing and could fall apart, the report said, citing people familiar with the matter.

OpenAI and Trail of Bits did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

OpenAI said on Friday it fired three researchers ⁠after an investigation ​found they had violated company policies on handling sensitive information.

The researchers, Jasmine Wang, Tomek ​Korbak and Mikita Balesni, had published a letter detailing the circumstances of their dismissal and arguing that the abrupt firings could create uncertainty among employees and undermine a culture in which researchers could ​raise safety concerns.

items.title: Six reasons Democrats may fall short of a midterm landslide in November
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Republican President Donald Trump's low approval ratings, voter concern over high prices and dissatisfaction with the Iran war have led many analysts and opinion polls to predict significant Democratic gains in the November 3 midterm elections.

But six analysts and party strategists told Reuters several factors could prevent Democrats from turning those favorable political conditions into a landslide, even if the party ultimately ​makes gains in Congress.

Here are six reasons Democrats may fall short of expectations.

The number of competitive US House races has shrunk sharply over the past ‌three decades as partisan polarization and redistricting – including gerrymandering – have made more seats safely Democratic or Republican.

As a result, analysts estimate that only about 40 to 50 of the House's 435 seats are truly competitive this year.

Most expect Democrats to retake the lower chamber, but with a majority of perhaps 5 to 20 seats, limiting the scope for gains like those in 2018, when Democrats picked up 41 seats.

Bill Galston, a former White House adviser to President Bill ​Clinton, said even if Democrats gain 25 House seats, "they'd have a working majority, but not a huge one."

Such a majority would give Democrats control of the House but little room ​to maneuver, making it harder to pass contentious legislation or claim the sweeping mandate associated with past wave elections.

While Democrats are ⁠favored to make gains in the 100-member Senate, achieving the net gain of four seats needed for a 51-49 majority remains far from certain because many of their top pickup targets are in ​states Trump carried by wide margins in 2024.

David Wasserman, an elections analyst at the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, said Democrats must make breakthroughs in states Trump carried by double digits. Even a national swing ​of 10 percentage points toward Democrats would likely leave the party two seats short of a majority, he said.

Democrats also face tougher-than-expected contests in states they had hoped would be safer, including Maine and Michigan.

"Republicans are hanging very close in those races," said Andrew Busch, a public policy professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and author of a history of midterm elections.

"That's not necessarily what you would expect if things were going well for Democrats across ​the board."

Opinion polls show Democratic voters more enthusiastic than Republicans, but strategists caution that such Democratic constituencies as young, Black and Hispanic voters have historically turned out at lower rates in midterm elections ​than in presidential years.

Surveys show persistent skepticism among these groups towards both parties, especially over the cost of living. If turnout among those groups falls short of expectations, Democrats could underperform on Election Day, they said.

In the ‌2022 midterms, ⁠voters aged 50 and older made up nearly twice as much of the electorate as those under 50. In recent years older voters have leaned Republican.

Republicans enter the campaign's final weeks with a substantial financial advantage, although spending in key races so far has had mixed results.

Republican national committees and allied congressional political action committees known as PACs held roughly $614 million in cash, compared with $392 million for Democrats, according to the latest Federal Election Commission filings.

Republicans are also drawing on Trump's MAGA Inc. super PAC, which held $416 million in cash at the beginning of September.

Republicans outspent Democrats by $188 million in Senate ​battleground advertising by the end of September, according ​to AdImpact, which tracks advertising spending.

"Any time ⁠you have one side with a big financial advantage and the ability to pour it into races at the last minute, it can tip the result of close races," Busch said.

Opinion polls have frequently underestimated Republican support in recent election cycles. Reuters/Ipsos polling shows registered voters favoring Democrats ​over Republicans by 43% to 35% on the congressional ballot.

The largest polling misses came when Trump was on the ballot. Trump, who is ​not on the ballot this ⁠year, has urged supporters to treat November's election as if he were.

Polls significantly understated Republican strength in the 2014 midterms, when the party won a sweeping Senate victory. Midterm polls in 2022 underestimated how well Democrats would perform.

Trump and many Republican candidates have sought to paint Democrats as socialists and extremists who pose an existential threat to the country.

Democrats in competitive races are increasingly declaring themselves proud capitalists, worried that ⁠the Republican tactics ​could sway critical independent voters.

Republicans are highlighting victories by members of the left-wing Democratic Socialists of America movement and ​progressive candidates in Democratic primaries to portray the whole party as socialist, even though fewer than two dozen of them scored wins this year.

Galston said the attacks could resonate with some wavering voters and influence close races.

"It might be effective at the ​margins," Galston said. "It could reduce the Democratic advantage by one or two points in the close races."

items.title: Mexico to require digital platforms to shield minors from harmful content
items.content_html:
MEXICO CITY, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said she will sign a presidential decree on Wednesday requiring digital platforms, ​including social media and streaming sites, to shield children and teenagers ‌from violent, sexual and other harmful content.

The decree, which will step up scrutiny of big technology companies in Latin America's second-largest economy, comes after an attack by two 18-year-old former students ​on a high school in the northern state of Coahuila in early ​October left one person dead and wounded three others.

Digital platforms will ⁠have one month to come into compliance with the decree, government adviser ​Luisa Maria Alcalde said.

Sheinbaum added that if companies failed to follow the decree, the ​government would back a bill to penalize the platforms.

Officials said they had already met with representatives of Meta (META.O), opens new tab, Microsoft (MSFT.O), opens new tab, Apple (AAPL.O), opens new tab, TikTok, Google (GOOGL.O), opens new tab, X and Huawei to discuss the matter.

A Meta spokesperson told ​Reuters that the company, which runs Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads, is "aware of ​the decree" and that it will "analyze it in detail," adding that it has long had ‌tools ⁠in place to help parents "guide their children's digital experience.”

"We will continue to engage with the authorities to help create a safer digital environment for teenagers in the country,” the spokesperson said, adding that Meta offers safety features on its platforms which ​include safeguards to ​limit who can ⁠make contact with children, as well as the monitoring of viewed content.

Microsoft, Apple, TikTok, Google, X and Huawei did not ​immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.

Mexico's move follows a ​broader global push ⁠to protect minors online, with governments in Europe and Australia tightening oversight of digital platforms and US states pursuing a range of child-safety measures.

Brazil has also moved ⁠to strengthen ​protections for children online. Such measures have raised ​questions over how to protect minors while safeguarding privacy and freedom of expression.

items.title: IMF calls for US to cut deficits amid bond woes, urges China to shift away from exports
items.content_html:
BANGKOK, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The United States cannot grow its way out of mounting public debt without tax or spending adjustments, while China must pivot from export-led growth towards more domestic consumption, International Monetary Fund ‌Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Wednesday.

Georgieva admonished the world's two largest economies to make painful policy changes to reduce growing fiscal and trade imbalances, as her fiscal affairs chief said inflation, high debt levels and rising yields had heightened the urgency for budget consolidation around the globe.

Speaking at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Georgieva singled out advanced economies, namely the US and European countries, as the "worst offenders" on excessive debts, with higher benchmark yields spilling over to low-income countries that have already been forced by financial ​markets to rein in borrowing.

Asked at a press conference whether the US needs tighter fiscal policy, Georgieva said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recognizes that US deficit and debt levels are too high and need to be ​made more sustainable.

"The authorities very much rely on strong growth in the United States" to help reduce debt, Georgieva said.

"At the Fund, we believe that growth of course helps, ⁠but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments. So, some (fiscal) measures would be necessary."

The call for more action to reduce debt was echoed in the IMF's Fiscal Monitor report on Wednesday, which warned that delays in an era of ​higher borrowing costs would only make the job harder in coming years.

While that message is a perennial one from the IMF, Rodrigo Valdes, the head of the IMF's Fiscal Affairs department, said the surge in bond yields had left governments ​with little fiscal room to manoeuvre.

"We dialled up the urgency of our message," he added.

Bessent is not attending the annual meetings in Bangkok, despite this year's US presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, instead favouring domestic engagements as the US midterm election campaign heats up.

He has acted as a chief spokesman for President Donald Trump's economic policies, particularly touting the deep tax cuts passed last year by Republicans now trying to maintain control of the US Congress.

G20 finance ministers are due to meet on the sidelines of ​the Bangkok meetings on Thursday. The US has used its G20 presidency to try to rally allies to take stronger action to counter China's "non-market" economic policies that have led to excess industrial capacity and a flood of global exports.

Asked ​about imbalances emanating from China, on a day when data showed it was on track to post a record trade surplus, Georgieva repeated longstanding advice to Beijing: "For surplus countries, what they need to do is increase domestic consumption. That clearly applies to China's ‌growth model. Shift ⁠from exports more toward domestic consumption."

Deficit countries need to save more and spend less, while Europe needs to invest more in competitiveness, she said.

"To put it very simply, China needs to spend more, the US has to save more, and Europe has to invest more," Georgieva added.

This week's meetings have been dominated by worries about growing debt and rising bond yields and risks from the artificial intelligence boom.

France, one of the advanced economies worst hit by a global bond sell-off, needs to solve its own debt woes through fiscal consolidation, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said, effectively playing down speculation about an ECB intervention in the bond market.

Asked at a CNN event in Bangkok whether the ECB was ​about to help France, Lagarde said it was up to ​Paris to soothe investors' nerves. "And for that one, the ⁠primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies," she said.

The IMF has lauded Britain for taking steps toward consolidation, but made clear on Wednesday that it does not want London to accelerate the pace of fiscal consolidation. "Our recommendation is 'stay the course'," Valdes said.

Still, OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann called for "strong fiscal ​discipline" in a statement to the IMF's steering committee, saying this was needed to ensure stability.

"In every G20 country except Germany and Türkiye, public debt as a ​share of GDP was higher in ⁠the first quarter of 2026 than at the end of 2007," he wrote to the International Monetary and Financial Committee.

"Countries need to contain and reallocate spending, improve public-sector efficiency and make tax systems more effective. They should also protect investment that drives future growth, especially in education, skills and digital infrastructure."

Regarding the growing divergence between advanced countries benefiting from AI investment and those bypassed by it, highlighted in Tuesday's IMF economic forecasts, Georgieva also urged IMF member countries to fully fund ⁠IMF facilities for ​low-income and vulnerable countries.

These include the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, which provides low- and zero-interest loans to low-income countries, and the Catastrophe ​Containment and Relief Trust, a fund that provides grants for debt-service relief and cancellation to the poorest and most vulnerable member countries, she said.

These countries, too, were being squeezed by higher bond yields, with average debt service costs that have increased to 14% of revenue from 6% a decade ​ago, even as overall debt burdens have eased, she said.

"The risk of divergence is most dangerous for those that are already further behind," Georgieva added.

items.title: Erie, Pennsylvania shooter killed 8 people, then himself, police say
items.content_html:
Oct 10 (Reuters) - A 45-year-old man shot and killed eight people in Erie, Pennsylvania, ​including a pregnant woman and two children, then apparently shot himself to ‌death, authorities said on Saturday at a press conference where they revealed details of the previous evening's shooting.

The shooter, who has yet to be identified, died of an apparent self-inflicted wound before officers arrived on ​the scene, said Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah.

"Some scenes stay with you long ​after you leave them. This is one of those tragic scenes," Lorah ⁠said.

Police have yet to establish a motive, Lorah said. He said eight of the nine ​who died in the shooting were family members, and one was a family friend.

Lorah said ​after the shooter entered the home, he came out of the house and shot two women who appeared "distressed" and were pacing back and forth seeking assistance from neighbors.

Police found the suspect on the second floor ​of the home on Perry Street, Lorah said.

Erie Mayor Daria Devlin said the police ​department "arrived at a horrific scene, faced unimaginable circumstances, and carried out their duties with courage and professionalism."

"They too ‌are ⁠members of this community, and they too will carry the weight of what happened last night," she said.

Earlier, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said in a statement on X that he had spoken with Mayor Devlin and had offered support following "the tragic mass shooting."

Shapiro has ​long advocated for "common sense ​gun safety," and pushed ⁠the Pennsylvania General Assembly in 2024 to pass gun reforms, including universal background checks and restrictions on ghost guns, which are homemade ​guns that lack serial numbers and cannot be traced. Several of ​Shapiro’s proposals have ⁠stalled in the state legislature.

There have been more than 400 mass shootings in the US in 2026, according to data compiled by Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting ⁠as one ​in which four or more people are shot, excluding ​the shooter. The last recorded mass shootings in Pennsylvania took place in July in Philadelphia, according to the ​data.

items.title: High gasoline prices expected to boost US consumer inflation in September
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - US consumer prices likely surged in September, driven by rising gasoline and food costs, and adding to a string of unfavorable developments for President ​Donald Trump and his Republican Party heading into crucial November 3 midterm elections.

The Labor Department's Consumer Price Index report on Wednesday will follow in the wake of surveys showing ‌a deterioration in consumer sentiment and a decline in Trump's approval rating amid frustration over the rising cost of living.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed about 78% of Americans blamed Trump's policies, including tariffs on imports and the US-Israeli war with Iran, for rising prices, which are outpacing wages. The CPI report is, however, expected to show a moderate increase in prices outside the volatile food and energy components over September, and further reduce the urgency for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again this month.

Economists said ​the slowdown in the monthly so-called core CPI inflation was of little comfort to consumers, especially those at the bottom of what they call the K-shaped economy.

"People care about food and energy. ​That's what they feel every day," said Sung Won Sohn, a finance and economics professor at Loyola Marymount University. "Many voters are at the lower leg of ⁠the K-shaped economy. They are suffering because of higher energy and food prices, and I assume that will have an impact on the election results, as a lot of people seem to think."

The CPI likely ​increased 0.6% last month after climbing 0.4% in August, a Reuters survey of economists predicted. Some estimated that gasoline could add roughly three-tenths of a percentage point to the CPI. Gasoline prices soared 7.1% in September, ​data from the US Energy Information Administration showed. Food prices are expected to have risen at least 0.2% after two straight monthly gains of 0.1%.

In the 12 months through September, the CPI is forecast to have increased 3.6% after rising 3.4% in August. The US central bank tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Indexes for its 2% inflation target.

The September CPI inflation report will be keenly awaited by millions of retirees and other Social Security recipients trying to figure out how ​much their benefits will increase next year. The Social Security Administration uses the CPI for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers data from the third quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2026 to ​determine the annual cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security and Supplemental Security Income benefits for 2027.

The programs benefit older Americans who have retired as well as the disabled and certain widows, widowers and children. The Senior Citizens League, one of ‌the nation's biggest ⁠seniors groups, is projecting a 3.5% COLA raise in 2027. That would be up from 2.8% in 2026, and would lift the average monthly benefit for retirees by $67.90 to $2,007.

The energy price shock is being closely watched for signs of broadening out beyond the transportation sector. Some economists said more expensive energy products were yet to become embedded into inflation, citing moderate increases in the core CPI. Others warned record high diesel prices, with no end in sight to the Middle East conflict, would soon feed through to higher prices at the supermarket. They pointed to elevated readings in the price measures in business surveys.

Excluding the volatile ​food and energy components, the CPI is expected to ​have gained 0.2% in September after climbing 0.3% ⁠in August. The anticipated moderation in core CPI inflation over the month would reflect the fading boost from a jump in mobile phone prices related to service changes at AT&T, though an above-expectations increase could not be ruled out. Other service providers raised their fees in September.

Airline fares likely increased further because of ​rising jet fuel prices. Moderate rises are expected for rents. Goods prices likely rose marginally as the impact of tariffs unwinds.

In the 12 months through ​September, core CPI inflation is ⁠forecast to have increased 2.5% after advancing 2.4% in August. This measure is lagging core PCE inflation, which increased 3.0% in August, because of the different weights assigned to the components in the baskets.

The Fed last month raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range, the first hike in three years, and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the months ahead. Financial markets assigned a roughly 22% chance of a ⁠rate hike at ​the October 27-28 policy meeting, CME's FedWatch Tool showed.

The odds of a rate increase this month were diminished by the underwhelming payroll ​gains in September as well as cooler-than-expected PCE inflation readings for July and August. Economists expect the Fed to raise rates in December.

"If the monthly core CPI rise manages to stay in the 0.2% range in September, that should be good enough for the Fed ​to hold in October," said Scott Anderson, chief US economist at BMO Capital Markets. "However, it won't settle the debate about whether more rate hikes are needed down the road."

items.title: Cornell bans fraternity parties for rest of academic year after alleged gang rape
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Cornell University will ban parties and social events at fraternity houses until the ‌end of the academic year, its president said on Tuesday, responding to the outcry over an alleged gang rape on campus in 2024.

The measure is the strongest reaction yet from Cornell's leadership to a lawsuit filed by a former undergraduate, Jane Doe, alleging seven men sexually assaulted her during a ​party.

Over the last several weeks, the Ivy League school in Ithaca, New York, and its president, Michael Kotlikoff, have ​come under heavy criticism from students, faculty and donors over its response to the allegations.

The suspension of ⁠parties and social events will apply to Interfraternity Council houses. The council website says Cornell currently has 34 fraternity houses.

"These measures will ​provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue," Kotlikoff ​said in the statement.

The Cornell Interfraternity Council did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Prosecutors reopened the investigation into the alleged gang rape after the lawsuit was filed. New York state Governor Kathy Hochul appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as an independent special prosecutor in the case, ​citing the earlier failure to protect the alleged victim.

President Donald Trump repeated on Tuesday his call to take James, his longtime ​critic and an elected Democrat, off the case.

"The Governor should take James off this case, immediately," Trump posted on Truth Social.

Trump first questioned James' ‌appointment ⁠in early October, but his comments did not prompt any action by officials. The offices of Hochul and the attorney general did not immediately reply to requests for comment.

Since the lawsuit against seven fraternity members, the university and others was filed in September, the Cornell administration has faced student protests, a pending no-confidence resolution from faculty, criticism by alumni and a public assembly where students blamed ​university officials for tolerating what they ​described as a culture of ⁠sexual violence.

None of the men named in the lawsuit have been criminally charged.

"I have spent the past weeks listening to students, faculty, staff, parents, alumni, and trustees, who have shared their feelings ​of deep connection and sympathy with Jane Doe, anger and frustration that this could happen ​at Cornell," Kotlikoff ⁠said.

"Women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe," he said, adding that additional staff would be hired to support survivors of sexual assault.

Cornell will also work with New York State Police to investigate incidents, he said, and accelerate previous recommendations put forward by a ⁠task force ​on sexual violence.

Thirty-five percent of undergraduate women reported experiencing non-consensual sexual contact ​involving force or incapacitation since entering Cornell, according to a university survey conducted in 2025 and published on its website.

"We must meet this moment by acknowledging where ​we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," Kotlikoff said.

items.title: US Supreme Court denies bid for pretrial release by anti-ICE activist
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to allow the pretrial release of an anti-ICE activist whose arrest for an allegedly threatening social ​media post during an immigration crackdown in Minneapolis was touted by President Donald Trump's administration in its campaign against "left-wing ‌agitators."

The justices denied self-described antifa, or "anti-fascist," member Kyle Wagner's request to revive a judge's ruling that ordered his pretrial release. Wagner was returned to custody after federal prosecutors appealed the judge's release order, arguing that he posed a danger to the community.

Wagner's lawyers argued in court papers that he was being ​unlawfully detained and noted that he has no violent criminal history.

Trump has made countering left-wing groups — and antifa in particular — ​a priority during his second term in office. The Republican president signed an executive order last year ⁠declaring the movement a "domestic terrorist organization" and has threatened to investigate and prosecute those who financially support it.

Wagner faces one count each ​of cyberstalking and transmitting interstate threats for his attempt to publish personal information, or "dox," a prominent online supporter of Trump's hardline immigration policies. ​Prosecutors cited other social media posts by Wagner — including his statement that the situation in Minneapolis was "kill or be killed" — as evidence of his dangerousness.

Wagner's arrest in Minneapolis on February 5 came during the Trump administration's large deployment of federal agents to the region in an immigration crackdown that spurred protests ​and led to the killing of two US citizens by immigration agents.

During a White House briefing that day, then-White House Press Secretary ​Karoline Leavitt displayed a printed photograph of a shirtless Wagner — who has tattoos on his face, neck and chest — and described him to reporters as ‌a "domestic ⁠terrorist."

"As for the left-wing agitators who have been illegally obstructing ICE's immigration efforts, we are not letting that behavior go unnoticed or unpunished," Leavitt said from the White House lectern. "In fact, just today, the Department of Homeland Security arrested this individual. He is a self-proclaimed antifa member who has been threatening, doxing, harassing ICE."

In August, the Cincinnati-based 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals granted the Justice Department's request ​to reverse US District Judge ​Denise Page Hood's pretrial release ⁠order.

Wagner's trial is scheduled to begin in January.

Judge Whitney Hermandorfer, a Trump appointee, wrote the 6th Circuit's 2-1 ruling that was joined by Judge Alan Norris, an appointee of Republican former President Ronald Reagan. ​The 6th Circuit ruled that the administration had made an adequate showing of Wagner's dangerousness.

In dissent ​was Judge Rachel ⁠Bloomekatz, an appointee of Democratic former President Joe Biden, who wrote that, "The government seldom appeals pretrial release orders, so why is it insistent here?"

Bloomekatz continued, "Wagner, who identifies as 'antifa' (anti-fascist) and has large tattoos on his face, neck and chest, looks aggressive in his social media videos, so it is ⁠no surprise ​that the White House press secretary held up a photo from one of ​his videos while touting law enforcement efforts against 'left-wing agitators.' ... But Wagner has never committed a violent crime."

In his Supreme Court filing, Wagner's lawyers told the justices that the ​6th Circuit's conclusion about his dangerousness was based on a "tendentious reading of Wagner's social media postings."

items.title: Fed Governor Cook's lawyer denounces Trump's latest attempt to remove her
items.content_html:
Oct 13 (Reuters) - Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook's lawyer questioned the objectivity of a White House probe into allegations she committed mortgage fraud, according to a letter seen by Reuters on Tuesday, challenging President Donald Trump's latest attempt to remove her from her role.

Trump has been trying to fire ​Cook for more than a year as he moves to exert more control over a central ​bank he says is refusing for political reasons to lower interest rates. Cook denies ⁠any wrongdoing and has sued to keep her job.

Earlier this month Trump announced a fresh inquiry into Cook ​and the appointment of a three-person committee to hold a hearing. The president later told reporters he would proceed ​with her firing if the committee recommended it. Cook's lawyers have said a fair hearing would show there is no legal basis for firing her.

In Tuesday's letter, Cook's lawyer, Abbe Lowell, noted that one of the proposed members of the committee, White House ​economic policy advisor Kevin Hassett, had previously pressured Cook to take leave from her office and suggested ​Trump had "cause" to fire her.

"A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of ‌any additional ⁠evidence – with no explanation for why it was not previously produced – is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence," Lowell wrote.

Lowell said Cook would not be able to attend a hearing on the November 5 date announced by the White House because she would be fulfilling her duties in Europe "at ​financial and monetary policy meetings."

The ​earliest that Cook could ⁠attend any hearing would be after the Fed's policy meeting scheduled for December 8-9, he wrote.

A Supreme Court ruling in Cook's case earlier this year barred ​Trump from firing a Fed governor at will, noting the need for the ​Fed to ⁠remain politically independent both in fact and in appearance in order to do its job.

But the ruling also laid out a path for a possible removal if a Fed official is given a fair chance to see the ⁠evidence of ​what is alleged and has a chance to refute it. The ​White House appears to be pursuing that path.

The Fed raised its policy rate in September and is expected to do so again at ​its final meeting of the year.

items.title: US Supreme Court to hear asylum fight involving Nigerian cook
items.content_html:
Oct 13 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court agreed on Tuesday to hear a bid by President Donald Trump's administration to deny asylum to a ​man who was forced to prepare meals for an apparent separatist group in Nigeria, in a case that could expand what officials ‌may deem terrorist activity under American immigration law.

The justices took up the Justice Department's appeal of a lower court's ruling in favor of Nigerian citizen Izuchukwu Ozurumba, who was denied US asylum due to his work cooking for a group known as the Unknown Gunmen that US officials considered to be a terrorist organization. The lower court ruled that cooking did ​not qualify as "material support" for terrorism under the immigration statute.

The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments and rule in the case by ​the end of June.

The administration, in appealing the case to the Supreme Court, said that if the lower court's ruling ⁠were allowed to stand, it would "substantially increase the burden on the government in excluding aliens with links to terrorism."

The case centers on whether Ozurumba's work ​for the group fell under provisions of US immigration law that bar the entry of non-US citizens who have "engaged in a terrorist activity," including actions that provide "material ​support" for such activity or "to a terrorist organization."

"At stake in this case is whether the government can use an overly broad reading of the law to shut the door on people seeking asylum," said Aimee Mayer-Salins, an attorney with the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, which is helping to represent Ozurumba.

The lower court "correctly recognized that asylum should not be denied ​to immigrants who provided no meaningful support to a terrorist group," Mayer-Salins added.

Following a job tip in 2022, Ozurumba took a van to a remote camp ​outside of Lagos, according to court papers. After he was hired, he eventually learned the camp was run by the Unknown Gunmen, a group likely associated with Nigerian separatists, ‌according to ⁠court papers.

Ozurumba soon "observed that the young men's movements from the camp coincided with news reports of murder and arson," his lawyers said in a court filing. Ozurumba sought to leave but was forced to stay without pay, they added.

After six months he escaped while on an outing for supplies, eventually making his way back to Lagos, they said.

Ozurumba then faced beatings and threats of death, prompting him to flee to Venezuela, where the threats continued, his lawyers said. Ozurumba then ​traveled to the southern US border ​and entered the country illegally in ⁠July 2023. Ozurumba eventually applied for asylum and other protections from deportation.

During Democratic former President Joe Biden's administration, an immigration judge deemed the Unknown Gunmen a terrorist organization and found that Ozurumba's cooking for the group rendered him ​inadmissible, and denied him any protections from deportation.

The judge concluded that the cooking helped the group accomplish its ​goals by satisfying their "basic ⁠human needs," and that it was irrelevant that he had worked under duress.

Ozurumba was deported back to Nigeria last year while his case was on appeal.

The Richmond, Virginia-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals sided with Ozurumba in September 2025, ruling that he was a captive laborer and his cooking did not constitute material support.

Ozurumba's work "provided ⁠nothing that ​the organization could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities," the ​4th Circuit ruled, but declined to order the government to return him to the US while the case proceeds.

"Providing meals to a terrorist organization's members is no less a material form of ​support than providing gasoline for its vehicles," the Justice Department told the Supreme Court in its appeal.

items.title: US televangelist Jim Bakker, ensnared in fraud and sex scandal, dead at 86
items.content_html:
Oct 5 (Reuters) - U.S. televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar empire and lived in opulence before being disgraced by a sex scandal, fraud conviction for bilking followers and divorce from television co-host Tammy Faye, died on Monday at age 86.

The death of ​Bakker, whose journey from the TV pulpit to a prison cell in the 1980s inspired comparisons to the corrupt character of the fictional preacher-huckster Elmer Gantry, was revealed on social media ‌by his second wife, Lori Bakker.

"It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening," she wrote on the Facebook and Instagram pages of her husband's latest television ministry.

She paid tribute to Bakker as a "pioneer of Christian television," but the cause and circumstances of his death were not revealed.

Bakker revived his career as a television preacher after prison with a new wife and new television show in 2003, later becoming a staunch supporter of ​President Donald Trump, who was known for his own brand of right-wing populism.

Bakker had been among the most popular of the Christian preachers who thrived on U.S. television in the 1980s, achieving fame on ​the show "The PTL Club." PTL stood for "Praise The Lord" and "People That Love."

Detractors, pointing to his unabashed daily exhortations to viewers for donations to his ministry, said PTL should ⁠have stood for "pass the loot."

Bakker spent 4-1/2 years in prison after being convicted in Charlotte, North Carolina, in 1989 of defrauding followers in a scheme involving vacations at his Heritage USA Christian theme park and resort.

Prosecutors painted him ​as a selfish and petty con man driven by greed and lust for power.

"Those of us who do have a religion are sick of being saps for money-grubbing preachers and priests," Judge Robert Potter told Bakker before sentencing ​him.

Bakker had quit the PTL ministry in 1987 after revelations of a 1980 sexual encounter with Jessica Hahn, a former church secretary who later posed nude in Playboy magazine, and a subsequent $265,000 payoff with ministry funds to gain her silence. Bakker was later defrocked.

Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker, his first wife, had started with a small TV ministry and eventually created a multimillion-dollar operation with 2,000 employees and the 2,300-acre (930-hectare) Heritage USA complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

At its peak, the PTL ministry drew 13 million viewers ​on 200 TV stations and raked in $129 million a year.

With his working-class upbringing, the affable Bakker related well to common folk.

He did not deliver fire-and-brimstone sermons like other televangelists, instead offering a friendly Christian message - although it was ​larded with requests for money donations.

Tammy Faye was more much more flamboyant, with her enthusiastic singing and penchant for tears that left her heavy makeup smeared on her face.

Bakker was convicted after a six-week trial in federal court on ‌all 24 fraud ⁠and conspiracy charges brought against him.

Prosecutors said he defrauded followers of $158 million by selling promises of lifetime annual vacations that he could not provide.

They said he siphoned $3.7 million to bankroll a lavish lifestyle that included several homes, luxury cars, mink coats, diamonds, servants - and an air-conditioned dog house.

The judge ordered Bakker to 45 years in prison but the sentence was later reduced. "I have sinned," Bakker told the court. "I have made mistakes. But never in my life did I intend to defraud anyone."

Bakker's chief aide, Richard Dortch, served 18 months of an eight-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to reduced charges in exchange for testifying against Bakker.

Tammy Faye was never charged. She stood by Bakker at the ​trial - even singing to reporters after his conviction - but ​divorced him in 1992 while he was in prison. ⁠She died of cancer in 2007.

Bakker started his life over after leaving prison in 1994, renouncing the "prosperity gospel" he once preached and writing a book titled "I Was Wrong."

"I've had a second chance at life. And I have a beautiful wife who loves me," Bakker told CNN in 2000, referring to his second wife, Lori, who he married ​in 1998.

They started a TV ministry together in 2003. In 2008, they began taping "The Jim Bakker Show" at a 600-acre (240-hectare) development called Morningside near the tourism city of ​Branson, Missouri, that bore similarities ⁠to Heritage USA.

Bakker once again pleaded with his followers for donations.

In 2020, he drew the ire of state and federal officials for selling a false treatment for COVID-19 during the deadly coronavirus pandemic.

Bakker also said in 2017 that Christians would launch a civil war if Trump were to be impeached. Trump later became the first U.S. president to be impeached twice.

James Orson Bakker was born on January 2, 1940, the son of an auto parts factory worker in Muskegon, Michigan, who ⁠maintained a strict ​fundamentalist Christian household.

He met Tammy Faye LaValley at North Central Bible College in Minneapolis and they married in 1961. Both dropped out of ​school to become traveling evangelists as he pursued the career of a minister of the Pentecostalist Assemblies of God denomination.

Their big break came in 1964, when televangelist Pat Robertson aired a children's religious puppet show with them on his fledgling TV network.

Setting out on his own ​in the 1970s, Bakker used the emerging world of cable and satellite TV to build an empire.
