items.title: US judge orders halt to taxpayer-funded ads featuring Trump
items.content_html:
Oct 11 (Reuters) - A US judge on Sunday blocked the Trump administration from using taxpayer money to pay for political ​advertisements, after publicly funded television ads glorifying US President Donald Trump began airing ‌in late September and sparked a bipartisan backlash.

Manhattan-based US District Judge Jennifer Rochon temporarily barred the advertisements after plaintiffs including watchdog group Common Cause brought a lawsuit alleging the ads were ​political propaganda designed to help Republican candidates in the November 3 midterm elections, ​not public service announcements.

The Trump administration was already planning to stop ⁠running the ads before Rochon's order, according to a separate statement filed with ​the court on Saturday.

The decision caps days of controversy over the taxpayer-funded advertisements, which ​were aired in the final weeks before the midterm elections.

“We won’t stop until this administration is held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste and abuse taxpayer funds ​for propaganda ever again," said Common Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomón.

Trump ​on Monday said he considered the ads to be a "positive promotion for our great U.S.A." but ‌that ⁠they would no longer be funded by taxpayers, and the White House said this week that the president's political action committee, MAGA PAC, would fund the ads going forward.

The White House said Trump's political action committee will not reimburse taxpayers for ​the ads that have ​already run. The ⁠ads end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government. The Justice Department did not immediately respond ​to a request for comment about the judge's order.

The plaintiffs, which also ​included a ⁠public employee union and a candidate for Alabama state representative, had asked Rochon to temporarily block the ads by Friday so that they could not air during weekend ⁠programming ​such as football games and Saturday Night Live.

Democratic Party ​officials also challenged the ads in a separate suit brought in federal court in Washington.

(This Oct 11 story has been repeated with no changes to the text.)

items.title: US military says it disabled cargo vessel trying to run Iran blockade
items.content_html:
Oct 10 (Reuters) - The US military ​said on Saturday it had disabled a commercial ‌cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman after the ship's crew ignored warnings and attempted to run a ​naval blockade against Iran.

"A U.S. military fighter jet ​struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean ⁠Molica (also known as the “Arika Sun”) with a precision ​munition, fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming the ​crew," the US Central Command posted on X.

CENTCOM said the cargo vessel had attempted to transit regional waters after ​leaving an Iranian port.

Reuters was not immediately able ​to reach the bulk carrier's operator for comment.

CENTCOM warned mariners in ‌the ⁠Gulf of Oman and the approaches to the Strait of Hormuz to heed blockade warnings, monitor notice-to-mariners broadcasts and contact US naval forces.

The number of ​vessels transiting the ​vital strait ⁠fell to the lowest in more than two months after attacks on tankers ​reached their highest level last week ​since the ⁠US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February, raising concerns over shipping disruptions and supporting crude ⁠prices.

Before ​the war, the Strait of ​Hormuz carried 20% of the world's oil consumption.

items.title: US to livestream Army firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 8 (Reuters) - The US will livestream the ​Army's upcoming firing squad execution of a gunman who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, the Pentagon said, in what would be an unprecedented ‌broadcast of a US execution.

Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, is set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945.

The execution is scheduled for December 3 at the same sprawling Texas base where Hasan opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility. It comes amid heightened debate in the US over the death penalty following the botched lethal injection of a Tennessee woman last week.

"It will be livestreamed. Details will follow," a Pentagon official ​told Reuters, speaking on the condition of anonymity.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who championed the push to execute Hasan by firing squad, confirmed plans to livestream the execution in an X post.

Media have ​sought to televise US executions in the past but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream a legal execution, ⁠experts said.

Public executions have become exceedingly rare worldwide. Among countries known to conduct them in recent years are Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan.

Extrajudicial lynchings in the United States, often by white mobs targeting Black Americans, were ​public spectacles well into the 20th century. The last legally sanctioned public execution in the United States was conducted in 1936, death penalty experts said. Thousands watched that 1936 hanging, opens new tab of a young Black man who had ​been convicted of raping a white woman.

Hegseth told the Human Events Daily program that deciding to execute Hasan by firing squad at Fort Hood on a Thursday at 1 p.m. — the approximate time, day of the week and location of the 2009 shooting — was a "no-brainer."

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public. Because people need to understand that ... there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.

Asked if Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth said: "Don't ​care. We'll see him on December 3."

A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder.

The shooting ​came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest.

Under US military law, a US president must approve ‌an execution by ⁠firing squad. President Donald Trump did so on Hegseth's recommendation, the Pentagon said on Monday.

The White House declined to say whether Trump supported the livestreaming, referring questions to the Pentagon.

The group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said Hasan's execution would be the first military execution since 1961.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging.

The last known executions by US military firing squads were in 1945, the center reported.

"It would be extremely, extremely strange" to livestream the event, said Eugene Fidell, a lawyer, author and military law expert who lectures at Yale Law School.

While firing squads have a long history in American ​military law, as far as he knew it would ​be unprecedented to livestream or televise an execution, ⁠Fidell said, adding that Hasan would need to sue in federal court if he wanted to block a public display of his death.

"The Supreme Court has never addressed this question, and it's an interesting question whether the current Supreme Court would put on their originalist hat and say, 'Well, it was OK in 1790, so ​what the hell?'" Fidell said.

Jonathan Lurie, an author and historian of military justice, said there are no compelling reasons to make the execution public.

"What's the ​point of it? Who would ⁠want to see that?" said Lurie.

At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In 2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years.

Death by firing squad is one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation.

The number of federal execution options ⁠was expanded in ​part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also sometimes proved challenging to carry out.

Plans by ​the state of Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel botched attempts to administer a lethal injection, leaving the death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but hospitalized.

Her lawyers said on Wednesday she ​awoke "angry and confused" in a hospital. Pike remains very sick and shackled to her hospital bed, they said.

items.title: India's Infosys does not expect material impact from US PERM suspension

items.title: The midterm strategy driving Democrats deep into Trump country
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 10 (Reuters) - On paper, Democrat Justin Pearson, a 31-year-old Tennessee state legislator, has little chance of winning the state's 9th Congressional District, which Republican lawmakers redrew months ago from a Democratic stronghold to a deeply Republican seat.

Yet this week the national Democratic Party added the rural district to its list of midterm targets in November, part of a broader strategy to ​compete in President Donald Trump's conservative heartland despite long odds of flipping it.

On its face, the strategy may look like Democratic overreach. Voters living in the 9th District's newly reconfigured boundaries, for instance, picked Trump by more than 21 points ‌in 2024.

More than a dozen Democratic operatives, strategists and candidates told Reuters the goal in part is to force Republicans to spend money defending safe seats, draining resources from the swing districts that will decide control of the US House.

By expanding the map, the party is also signaling to donors that races are becoming more competitive amid high prices and the Iran war driving Trump's unpopularity, helping unlock money that might otherwise stay on the sidelines, they said.

"These expansions force Republicans to go on defense in more districts," said one House campaign official, speaking on the condition of anonymity. "It's also a signal to donors and outside groups ​that House Democrats are taking these races seriously."

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the party's US House campaign arm, this week added Pearson's race and 13 others to its target list, expanding its battlefield to 66 Republican-held ​seats.

Getting on the target list gives candidates access to national party staff and campaign tools, while also raising their profiles with donors, potentially opening new streams of fundraising for their campaigns.

There are early ⁠signs the strategy is having some effect. Republican-aligned groups have begun spending in some newly added districts, while two Democratic campaigns in Republican districts told Reuters their fundraising accelerated after being placed on the target list.

Republicans have dismissed the idea that Democrats have a serious chance ​of defeating their party in districts that overwhelmingly voted for Trump in 2024.

Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee - the party's House campaign group - accused the Democratic Party of "stretching its map a mile wide and an inch deep, pretending every district in America is ​suddenly a battleground." He said the strategy will force Democrats to spend in long-shot contests when the party is already being outspent by Republicans.

Analysts, too, are skeptical.

"I'll take it seriously when they actually put their money where their mouth is. There is a point at which it becomes fantasy land," said David Wasserman, an elections analyst at the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, which rates many of these races as safely Republican.

Democrats say they have chosen these districts for a number of reasons, including the quality of their candidates and the chance they might pull off upset wins to increase the size of ​a potential House majority.

It remains unclear how much money Democrats will ultimately devote to the newly added districts. Recent campaign finance filings are not yet available, and the party declined to tell Reuters where it is spending or how much it plans to ​spend on its expanded map.

But there are signs Republicans are paying attention. Restoration of America PAC, funded primarily by billionaire Richard Uihlein, spent nearly $750,000 on digital ads backing Republican David Flippo in Nevada's 2nd District last week, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

The district, which Trump carried by ‌14 points in ⁠2024, is among the recent additions to the Democratic target list.

"Democrats are on offense, Republicans are running scared, even in deep-red territory, and our expansive map reflects it," DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene said in a statement.

The new target list includes districts in Arkansas, New York and Virginia that Trump carried by as many as 24 points. Democrats say rising costs and dissatisfaction with some Trump policies are creating openings in rural and Republican-leaning areas.

"Rural America is unhappy with tariffs and rising fuel and farm costs, and that's pushing us into redder areas," Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said.

Democrats will need a net gain of four to retake the House. However, only about 50 of the 435 House races are expected to be competitive.

Tennessee Republicans in May split the heavily Democratic Memphis area into three districts, transforming the 9th from ​a majority-Black urban seat into a sprawling district stretching more than 200 ​miles (322 km) across rural western Tennessee, a change that made ⁠the seat significantly more favorable to Republicans.

Yet Pearson says he has found independent and Republican voters frustrated by the high cost of living who are open to voting Democratic.

"We've traveled across all 15 counties, filling churches and community centers in places people said we couldn't compete," said Pearson, a Black lawmaker who gained national attention in 2023 when the Republican-majority legislature expelled him for joining a gun-violence protest at ​the state Capitol.

Republicans have portrayed Pearson as an outspoken progressive activist, pointing to his participation in gun-control and voting-rights protests.

"The people in Tennessee Nine, they have a clear choice. They can ​choose confidence over chaos, and they ⁠can choose common sense over communism, and they can choose a lawmaker over a troublemaker," his Republican opponent, state senator Brent Taylor, told Reuters.

There has been little public polling on the race, which Cook rates "Solid Republican."

Being added to the target list can quickly pay dividends for a campaign. Candidates or representatives from four Democratic campaigns on the DCCC's list told Reuters they either expected to see a boost in donations or were already seeing an uptick since their addition.

Pearson said his campaign has seen a surge of financial support after being added to the list, which ⁠would boost his ​get-out-the-vote operation.

"This race is going to be tight. It's going to be close. It's going to come down to how many people can we see before Election ​Day, knocking on those doors and reaching out to them directly," he said.

But Democrats' ambitions are constrained by a relative cash shortage.

While Democratic candidates nationally have outraised their Republican opponents, Republican national party committees and Republican-aligned super PACs have far outstripped Democratic counterparts in money raised.

Democrats in tough races in the expanded map said they are ​connecting with small-dollar donors by focusing on cost-of-living issues and campaigning heavily at town halls and other local appearances.

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: US imposes sanctions on ICC hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
items.content_html:
Oct 9 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the ​International Criminal Court on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies.

The court denounced the ‌move as an "assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order," and called on its 125 member states to take action to defend it.

"The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it," it said in a statement. "This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law. History will judge this moment."

The Trump ​administration has long been hostile to the court, founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges.

Friday's move goes much ​further, potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself, amounting to an unprecedented attack on an institution founded on an international treaty. The ⁠US initially signed the Rome Statute that founded the court but never ratified it.

"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement, ​first published by Reuters.

"That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate."

The US Treasury announced the sanctions with a six-month initial grace period, and some other exemptions that would allow some transactions for telecoms, software, payment of pensions and transactions related to detainees.

Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns, and would be adjusted if those demands were not met.

Washington has denounced the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and ​an investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC says is "deprioritized."

Rubio in his statement cited calls from outside experts for the ICC to prosecute American service members, border patrol agents and ​elected leaders. ICC officials have not taken steps toward such prosecutions.

"The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing," ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan told ‌Reuters. "Our work ⁠will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions."

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on social media that the six-month period "offers a window for dialogue" but added that the bloc "has options to ensure that (the ICC) can continue its vital work." Belgium's foreign minister called for an EU blocking statute to be activated to protect the court.

The ICC has issued arrest warrants against more than 70 people, including world leaders and major figures in global conflicts. In addition to Netanyahu, it has sought the arrest of Hamas figures. Others who were the subject of arrest warrants include Russian President Vladimir Putin, former Sudan President ​Omar al-Bashir and former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi. ​Charges against Kenyan President William Ruto and former ⁠Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta were withdrawn.

Despite US calls for countries to quit the court, it has received strong backing from most member states, which include all EU countries and all members of the NATO alliance apart from the United States and Turkey. It is based in ​the Netherlands, an EU and NATO member.

The Nobel Prize awarded hours earlier to South African jurist Navi Pillay, who sat on the ICC's Appeals ​Chamber from 2003-2008, was explicitly ⁠described by the prize committee as a gesture of support for such tribunals at a time when "judges and institutions of international law are under political attack".

"An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world," the prize committee said.

US sanctions typically bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organization, forcing banks to shut accounts, ⁠insurers to end ​coverage and software companies to halt cooperation.

The Trump administration previously imposed targeted sanctions on court officials during his first term, ​which were rescinded under President Joe Biden. Washington announced new sanctions just days after Trump returned to office in January 2025.

Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of sanctions on the court itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open-source ​equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.
